EXISTING UTILITY INFORMATION SHOWN IS FOR INFORMATIONAL PURPOSES ONLY. IT IS DERIVED FROM ON-SITE SURVEY AND/OR
UTILITY MAPPING PROVIDED TO THE ENGINEER, AND THEREFORE UTILITIES MAY NOT BE LOCATED CORRECTLY, EITHER
HORIZONTALLY OR VERTICALLY, AND MAY NOT BE ALL INCLUSIVE. CONTRACTOR IS REQUIRED TO FOLLOW THE PROCEDURE
OUTLINED BELOW:
16.1.
CONTRACTOR IS REQUIRED TO LOCATE AND POTHOLE ALL EXISTING UTILITY LINES (BOTH HORIZONTALLY AND VERTICALLY)
THAT AFFECT THE PROJECT CONSTRUCTION, EITHER ON-SITE OR OFF-SITE, AND DETERMINE IF THERE ARE ANY CONFLICTS
WITH THE DESIGN OF THE SITE AS SHOWN ON THE APPROVED PLANS PRIOR TO ANY CONSTRUCTION. IF IT IS DETERMINED
THAT CONFLICTS EXIST BETWEEN EXISTING UTILITIES AND DESIGN UTILITIES (OR ANOTHER ASPECT OF PROPOSED
CONSTRUCTION) THE ENGINEER MUST BE NOTIFIED IMMEDIATELY TO CORRECT THE CONFLICTS BEFORE ANY WORK CAN BEGIN.
IF THE CONTRACTOR FAILS TO FOLLOW THIS ABSOLUTE REQUIREMENT AND CONFLICTS ARISE DURING CONSTRUCTION THE
CONTRACTOR WILL BEAR THE SOLE RESPONSIBILITY TO FIX THE CONFLICTS.
16.2.
CONTRACTOR IS REQUIRED TO VERIFY THAT PROPER COVER AND PROTECTION OF EXISTING UTILITY LINES IS MAINTAINED OR
ATTAINED WITHIN THE DESIGN ONCE VERIFICATION OF THE EXISTING UTILITIES IS COMPLETED AS OUTLINED IN 16.1 ABOVE.
16.3.
IN ADDITION TO 16.1 AND 16.2 ABOVE THE CONTRACTOR WILL VERIFY DEPTHS OF UTILITIES IN THE FIELD BY "POTHOLING" A
MINIMUM OF 300 FEET AHEAD OF PROPOSED PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION TO AVOID POTENTIAL CONFLICTS WITH DESIGNED
PIPELINE ALIGNMENT AND GRADE AND EXISTING UTILITIES.
16.4.
IF A CONFLICT ARISES BETWEEN EXISTING UTILITIES AND DESIGN UTILITIES (OR ANOTHER ASPECT OF PROPOSED
CONSTRUCTION) AS DETERMINED UNDER 16.1, 16.2 OR 16.3 THE CONTRACTOR WILL NOTIFY THE ENGINEER IMMEDIATELY TO
RESOLVE THE CONFLICT.
16.5.
IF A CONFLICT ARISES BETWEEN EXISTING UTILITIES AND DESIGN UTILITIES (OR ANOTHER ASPECT OF PROPOSED
CONSTRUCTION) RESULTING FROM THE CONTRACTOR'S NEGLIGENCE TO IDENTIFY AND/OR “POTHOLE” EXISTING UTILITIES AS
REQUIRED IN 16.1, 16.2 AND 16.3 ABOVE, THE CONTRACTOR WILL BE REQUIRED TO RESOLVE THE CONFLICT WITHOUT
ADDITIONAL COST OR CLAIM TO THE OWNER OR ENGINEER.

EXISTING UTILITIES HAVE BEEN SHOWN ON THE PLANS BASED ON ON-SITE SURVEY. PRIOR TO COMMENCING ANY WORK, IT
SHALL BE THE CONTRACTOR'S RESPONSIBILITY TO HAVE EACH UTILITY COMPANY LOCATE, IN THE FIELD, THEIR MAIN AND
SERVICE LINES. THE CONTRACTOR SHALL NOTIFY BLUE STAKES AT 1-800-662-4111 48 HOURS IN ADVANCE OF PERFORMING
ANY EXCAVATION WORK. THE CONTRACTOR SHALL RECORD THE BLUE STAKES ORDER NUMBER AND FURNISH ORDER
NUMBER TO OWNER AND ENGINEER PRIOR TO ANY EXCAVATION. IT WILL BE THE CONTRACTOR'S SOLE RESPONSIBILITY TO
DIRECTLY CONTACT ANY OTHER UTILITY COMPANIES THAT ARE NOT MEMBERS OF BLUE STAKES. IT SHALL BE THE
CONTRACTOR'S SOLE RESPONSIBILITY TO PROTECT ALL EXISTING UTILITIES SO THAT NO DAMAGE RESULTS TO THEM
DURING THE PERFORMANCE OF THIS CONTRACT. ANY REPAIRS NECESSARY TO DAMAGED UTILITIES SHALL BE PAID FOR BY
THE CONTRACTOR. THE CONTRACTOR SHALL BE REQUIRED TO COOPERATE WITH OTHER CONTRACTORS AND UTILITY
COMPANIES INSTALLING NEW STRUCTURES, UTILITIES AND SERVICE TO THE PROJECT.

J. SEWER MAIN AND LATERAL CONSTRUCTION REQUIREMENTS SLC PUBLIC UTILITIES MUST APPROVE ALL SEWER CONNECTIONS. ALL SEWER LATERALS 6-INCHES
AND SMALLER MUST WYE INTO THE MAINS PER SLC PUBLIC UTILITIES REQUIREMENTS. ALL 8-INCH
AND LARGER SEWER CONNECTIONS MUST BE PETITIONED FOR AT PUBLIC UTILTIES (483-6762) AND
CONNECTED AT A MANHOLE. INSIDE DROPS IN MANHOLES ARE NOT ALLOWED. A MINIMUM 4-FOOT
BURY DEPTH IS REQUIRED ON ALL SEWER MAINS AND LATERALS. CONTRACTOR SHALL INSTALL
INVERT COVERS IN ALL SEWER MANHOLES WITHIN THE PROJECT AREA.
CONTRACTOR TO PROVIDE AIR PRESSURE TESTING OF SEWER MAINS IN ACCORDANCE WITH PIPE
MANUFACTURERS RECOMMENDATIONS AND SALT LAKE CITY PUBLIC UTILITIES REQUIREMENTS. ALL
PVC SEWER MAIN AND LATERAL TESTING SHALL BE IN ACCORDANCE WITH UNI-BELL UN-B-6-98
RECOMMENDED PRACTICE FOR LOW PRESSURE AIR TESTING OF INSTALLED SEWER PIPE.
CONTRACTOR SHALL PROVIDE SEWER LATERAL WATER TESTING AS REQUIRED BY THE SALT LAKE
CITY PUBLIC UTILITIES PROJECT ENGINEER OR INSPECTOR. A MINIMUM OF 9-FEET OF HEAD
PRESSURE IS REQUIRED AS MEASURED VERTICALLY FROM THE HIGH POINT OF THE PIPELINE AND AT
OTHER LOCATIONS ALONG THE PIPELINE AS DETERMINED BY THE SLC PUBLIC UTILITIES PROJECT
ENGINEER OR INSPECTOR. TESTING TIME WILL BE NO LESS THAN AS SPECIFIED FOR THE AIR TEST
DURATION IN TABLE I ON PAGE 12 OF UNI-B-6-98. ALL PIPES SUBJECT TO WATER TESTING SHALL BE
FULLY VISIBLE TO THE INSPECTOR DURING TESTING. TESTING MUST BE PERFORMED IN THE
PRESENCE OF A SLC PUBLIC UTILITIES REPRESENTATIVE. ALL VISIBLE LEAKAGE MUST BE REPAIRED
TO THE SATISFACTION OF THE SLC PUBLIC UTILITIES ENGINEER OR INSPECTOR.
K. WATER AND FIRE MAIN AND SERVICE CONSTRUCTION REQUIREMENTS SLC PUBLIC UTILITIES MUST APPROVE ALL FIRE AND WATER SERVICE CONNECTIONS. A MINIMUM
3-FOOT SEPARATION IS REQUIRED BETWEEN ALL WATER AND FIRE SERVICE TAPS INTO THE MAIN. ALL
CONNECTIONS MUST BE MADE MEETING SLC PUBLIC UTILITIES REQUIREMENTS. A 5-FOOT MINIMUM
BURY DEPTH (FINAL GRADE TO TOP OF PIPE) IS REQUIRED ON ALL WATER/FIRE LINES UNLESS
OTHERWISE APPROVED BY PUBLIC UTILITIES. WATER LINE THRUST BLOCK AND RESTRAINTS ARE AS
PER SLC APPROVED DETAIL DRAWINGS AND SPECIFICATIONS. ALL EXPOSED NUTS AND BOLTS WILL
BE COATED WITH CHEVRON FM1 GREASE PLUS MINIMUM 8 MIL THICKNESS PLASTIC. PROVIDE
STAINLESS STEEL NUTS, BOLTS AND WASHERS FOR HIGH GROUNDWATER/ SATURATED CONDITIONS
AT FLANGE FITTINGS, ETC.
ALL WATERLINES INSTALLATIONS AND TESTING TO BE IN ACCORDANCE WITH AWWA SECTIONS C600,
C601, C651, C206, C200, C900, C303 AWWA MANUAL M11 AND ALL OTHER APPLICABLE AWWA, UPWS,
ASTM AND ANSI SPECIFICATIONS RELEVANT TO THE INSTALLATION AND COMPLETION OF THE
PROJECT. AMENDMENT TO SECTION C600 SECTION 4.1.1; DOCUMENT TO READ MINIMUM TEST
PRESSURE SHALL NOT BE LESS THAN 200 P.S.I. GAUGED TO A HIGH POINT OF THE PIPELINE BEING
TESTED. ALL MATERIALS USED FOR WATERWORKS PROJECTS TO BE RATED FOR 150 P.S.I. MINIMUM
OPERATING PRESSURE.

INDIVIDUAL PROPERTY OWNER(S) FOR WORK OR STAGING OUTSIDE OF THE PROJECT LIMITS.

OF SUBSURFACE DRAIN LINES AND GEOTEXTILE, AND OVEREXCAVATION OF UNSUITABLE BEARING MATERIALS
AND PLACEMENT OF ACCEPTABLE FILL MATERIAL.

EXISTING UNDERGROUND UTILITIES AND IMPROVEMENTS ARE SHOWN IN THEIR APPROXIMATE LOCATIONS
BASED UPON RECORD INFORMATION AVAILABLE AT THE TIME OF PREPARATION OF THESE PLANS. LOCATIONS
MAY NOT HAVE BEEN VERIFIED IN THE FIELD AND NO GUARANTEE IS MADE AS TO THE ACCURACY OR
COMPLETENESS OF THE INFORMATION SHOWN. IT SHALL BE THE RESPONSIBILITY OF THE CONTRACTOR TO
DETERMINE THE EXISTENCE AND LOCATION OF THE UTILITIES SHOWN ON THESE PLANS OR INDICATED IN THE
FIELD BY LOCATING SERVICES. ANY ADDITIONAL COSTS INCURRED AS A RESULT OF THE CONTRACTOR'S
FAILURE TO VERIFY THE LOCATIONS OF EXISTING UTILITIES PRIOR TO THE BEGINNING OF CONSTRUCTION IN
THEIR VICINITY SHALL BE BORNE BY THE CONTRACTOR AND ASSUMED INCLUDED IN THE CONTRACT. THE
CONTRACTOR IS TO VERIFY ALL CONNECTION POINTS WITH THE EXISTING UTILITIES. THE CONTRACTOR IS
RESPONSIBLE FOR ANY DAMAGE CAUSED TO THE EXISTING UTILITIES AND UTILITY STRUCTURES THAT ARE TO
REMAIN. IF CONFLICTS WITH EXISTING UTILITIES OCCUR, THE CONTRACTOR SHALL NOTIFY THE ENGINEER
PRIOR TO CONSTRUCTION TO DETERMINE IF ANY FIELD ADJUSTMENTS SHOULD BE MADE.

2196 E 6450 S Stormwater Calculations

COTTONWOOD HEIGHTS CITY
PLANNING COMMISSION
STAFF MEMO
October 21, 2026
Summary
This is a city-initiated request for a zoning text amendment to update standards in the Cottonwood
Heights Municipal Code (CHMC) Chapter 19.75: Accessory Dwelling Units. The proposed
amendments are intended to bring Chapter 19.75 into compliance with S.B. 284, which enacted
Utah Code Section 10-21-304, establishing requirements and limits for municipal regulation of
detached ADUs. The principal changes address permitted-use approval of detached ADUs, expand
eligible zoning districts, and remove the internal ADU minimum-lot-size exclusion.

Background
Utah Code Section 10-21-304 became effective October 1, 2026. It requires municipalities to permit
a detached ADU on a lot or parcel of at least 11,000 square feet that contains a single-family
dwelling, provided the single-family dwelling is a permitted use. Municipalities may also permit
detached ADUs on smaller lots.
Utah Code 10-21-304 requires compliance with applicable building, health, and fire codes and a
process for converting a legally constructed accessory structure into a detached ADU, subject to
applicable setbacks and code requirements. Permitted use status therefore does not eliminate site
review, construction permits, or safety inspections.
The state framework still allows cities to regulate detached ADU structure size, dimensions, height,
lot coverage, and setbacks, subject to statutory limitations. It also allows an owner-occupancy
requirement under which the owner resides in either the single-family dwelling or the detached ADU
and allows a limit of one ADU per lot or parcel.
The existing Cottonwood Heights Municipal Code distinguishes internal ADUs from detached ADUs.
Internal ADU eligibility is limited to lots larger than 6,000 square feet in the R-1, RR-1, and F-1 zones,
while detached ADUs require conditional approval. Detached approval currently includes Planning
Commission review and a public hearing. Annual inspection and renewal provisions are also part of
the local administrative framework.

Proposed Changes
The table below summarizes the key differences between existing and proposed ADU regulations.
Proposed changes address both updated Utah Code requirements and local policy choices
intended to simplify the review process. Changes not specifically required by Utah Code, but
proposed at the local level, are marked with an asterisk (*).

1. CHMC Chapter 19.75 – Tracked Changes
2. Utah State Code 10-21-303 – Internal Accessory Dwelling Units
3. Utah State Code 10-21-304 – Detached Accessory Dwelling Units

19.75.010 Purpose
Accessory dwelling units (“ADUs”) in single-family residential zones are an important tool
in the overall housing goals and needs of the city, and allow for alternative and flexible
housing options in owner-occupied single-family residences. The purposes of the ADU
standards of this chapter are to:
A. Preserve and enhance life safety standards required for residential occupancy
through the creation of a regulatory process for ADUs;
B. Provide housing options for individuals and families in all stages of life and/or with
moderate income who might otherwise have difficulty finding adequate housing
within the city;
C. Provide opportunities to offset rising housing costs and promote reinvestment in
existing single-family residential zones;
D. Preserve the character of single-family neighborhoods through adequate standards
governing ADUs; and
E. Comply with UTAH CODE ANN. 10-9a-530 10-21-303 and 10-21-304, which
designates internal and detached ADUs as permitted uses in all zones that allow
single-family dwellings single-family residential zones and imposes limitations on
the extent that municipalities may regulate ADUs.
19.75.020 Definitions
“Accessory dwelling unit” or “ADU” means a permanent, residential dwelling unit meant for
one additional single family located in a separate dwelling unit on the same lot as a singlefamily dwelling unit, either within the same building as the single-family dwelling unit or in a
detached accessory building. A mobile home (as defined in UTAH CODE ANN. 57-16-3, as
amended) or other portable structure does not qualify as an ADU, nor may an ADU be
located within a mobile home or other portable structure.
“Detached ADU” means an ADU located in an accessory building on the property and not
attached to or within the principal dwelling unit.
“Dwelling unit” means a portion of a building designated as the residence of one family or
individual with suitable approved provisions for eating, sleeping, cooking, and sanitation.
“Flag lot” means a lot not fronting on or abutting a public roadway and where access to the
public roadway is limited to a narrow private right-of-way.

“Internal ADU” means an ADU created (a) within a primary dwelling unit; (b) within the
footprint of the primary dwelling unit at the time the internal ADU is created; and (c) for the
purpose of offering a long-term rental of 30 consecutive days or longer.
“Owner occupancy” means that a property’s owner of record makes such owner’s legal
residence at the site for at least 200 days per calendar year, as evidenced by voter
registration, vehicle registration, driver’s license, county assessor records or similar
means.
“Primary dwelling” means a single-family dwelling that (a) is detached; and (b) is occupied
as the primary residence of the owner of record.
“Short-term rental” means the rental, letting of rooms or sub-leasing/renting of any
structure, dwelling or portion thereof for occupancy, dwelling, lodging or sleeping purposes
for fewer than 30 consecutive days in duration.
HISTORY
Adopted by Ord. 368 on 9/21/2021
19.75.030 Where Permitted
A. Internal ADUs are permitted in primary dwellings under owner occupancy on lots
containing more than 6,000 square feet located a single-family primary dwelling in
the city’s R-1 (single-family), RR-1 (rural residential), R-2-8 (multi-family), RM (multifamily), RO (residential office), and F-1 (foothill residential) zones, subject to the
approval process detailed in this chapter. Internal ADUs are prohibited on any lot
containing 6,000 or fewer square feet, or on lots where the primary dwelling is
served by a failing septic tank. Internal ADUs in eligible areas shall be allowed as
permitted uses.
B. Detached ADUs may be allowed as conditional uses are permitted on lots
containing an owner-occupied single-family primary dwelling in the city’s R-1
(single-family), RR-1 (rural residential), R-2-8 (multi-family), RM (multi-family), RO
(residential office), and F-1 (foothill residential) zones as provided in this chapter., or
in any other zone in which a single-family dwelling is a permitted use, subject to the
approval process detailed in this chapter. Detached ADUs are prohibited on any lot
where the primary dwelling is served by a failing septic tank. Detached ADUs in
eligible areas shall be allowed as permitted uses.
HISTORY
Adopted by Ord. 368 on 9/21/2021
19.75.040 Approval Process

The approval process for ADUs in the city is as follows:
A. An internal ADU is allowed may be allowed as a permitted use upon completion and
filing of an ADU application form; payment of all applicable fees; completion of a
satisfactory property inspection; the city’s receipt of the completed, signed affidavit
required by this chapter; issuance of any necessary building permits; and
compliance with all other applicable requirements of this chapter. Permits for
internal, compliant ADUs may be renewed annually upon a satisfactory property
inspection and payment of an administrative renewal fee. A portion of a principal
dwelling unit or a detached structure with the characteristics of a separate dwelling
unit but not occupied by a second family is exempt from obtaining an ADU permit
and from paying the yearly renewal fee upon completion and recordation of an
exemption form provided by the city. Internal ADUs shall comply with all other
applicable building permit, zoning code, fire code and building code requirements.
B. A detached ADU may be allowed as a conditional use upon completion and filing of
an ADU application form; payment of all applicable fees; completion of a
satisfactory property inspection; the city’s receipt of the completed, signed affidavit
required by this chapter; issuance of any necessary building permits; compliance
with all other applicable requirements of this chapter and any additional
requirements deemed necessary by the planning commission (and approval by the
planning commission following a public hearing). Permits for detached ADUs may
be renewed annually upon a satisfactory property inspection and payment of a
renewal fee. A detached structure with the characteristics of a separate dwelling
unit but not occupied by a second family is exempt from obtaining an ADU permit
and from paying the yearly renewal fee upon completion and recordation of an
exemption form provided by the city. Detached ADU units shall comply with all other
applicable building permit, zoning code, fire code and building code requirements.
19.75.050 Development Standards
A. The property’s record owner (including titleholders and contract purchasers) must
occupy either the primary dwelling unit or the approved ADU as such owner’s
permanent residence and at no time receive rent for the owner-occupied unit. For
an internal ADU, this requirement operates as a prohibition on renting the internal
ADU when the primary dwelling is not occupied as the owner’s primary residence.
An application for an ADU permit shall include evidence of owner occupancy in the
form of the affidavit required by Section 19.75.060 and such other verification(s) as
the city reasonably may require.

B. ADUs shall not be used as short-term rentals.
C. Only one ADU may be created per lot or property.
D. The design and size of the ADU shall conform to all current applicable standards in
the building, plumbing, electrical, mechanical, fire, health, and any other applicable
codes. When a new internal ADU is proposed in an existing home, the entire internal
ADU shall be brought up to all minimum standards, as inspected and approved by
city staff.
E.
1. The installation of separate utility meters for an internal ADU is prohibited.
2. The installation of separate utility meters for a detached ADU is permitted,
provided:
a) The applicant demonstrates, with supporting documentation from the
applicable utility provider, that the existing utilities cannot be
adequately sized for the ADU or that bifurcation from the principal
residence cannot be reasonably achieved; and
b) The property’s record owner remains responsible for all utility billings
associated with both the primary dwelling and the ADU.
F. Each internal ADU shall require one off-street parking space in addition to required
parking for the primary dwelling unit. In no case shall fewer than three total offstreet parking stalls be provided for any property with an internal ADU. The
additional required parking space shall not be located behind or in front one of the
required parking spaces for the primary dwelling (i.e., tandem parking is prohibited).
G. Each detached ADU shall require two off-street parking spaces in addition to
required parking for the primary dwelling unit. Creation of additional off-street
parking spaces, excluding previously existing driveways, is prohibited in the front
yard of the subject property. Additional required parking spaces for detached ADUs
shall not be located behind or in front of one of the required parking spaces for the
primary dwelling or the detached ADU (i.e., tandem parking is prohibited).
H. Any parking spaces contained within a garage or carport shall be replaced if an
internal ADU is created within the garage or carport.
I. Each internal ADU shall be designed in a manner that does not change the
appearance of the primary dwelling as a single-family dwelling.

J. An internal ADU may not be created within a mobile home as defined in UTAH CODE
ANN. 57-16-3, as amended.
K. Detached ADUs shall be required to install fencing and/or a landscaping buffer to
mitigate the impact of parking areas and ADU entrances from adjoining property
owners. Fencing shall be a solid visual barrier and shall comply with applicable
fencing requirements. Landscaping shall be designed to obstruct visual impact from
adjoining properties. In considering detached ADUs, the planning commission may
require additional buffering requirements if it finds that such requirements will
mitigate a perceived negative impact created by the ADU.
L. Detached ADUs shall be subject to the following additional development standards:
1. Any detached ADU shall be a permanent structure. Trailers, mobile homes,
and other portable structures shall not be permitted as detached ADUs. The
city’s building official shall make the determination of whether or not a
structure is permanent.
2. Any detached ADU shall be located in the rear yard of a property and shall
maintain a setback of at least six feet from the primary structure;
3. Any detached ADU shall be subject to primary structure side and rear
setback standards for the zone in which it is located;
4. Any detached ADU shall meet all accessory building standards for height, lot
coverage, rear-yard coverage, size, and any other applicable standards for
the zone in which it is located;
5. Any detached ADU on a flag lot shall meet primary structure flag lot setback
standards for the zone in which it is located; and
6. Conversion of existing accessory buildings to detached ADUs is only
permitted if the structure meets or is modified to meet all current city
standards and all applicable provisions of this chapter. The owner of a legally
constructed accessory structure may convert the structure to a detached
ADU through the approval process set forth in Section 19.75.040, subject to
applicable dwelling and accessory structure setback requirements and all
applicable building, health, and fire codes.
19.75.060 Affidavit
All applications for ADU permits shall include a notarized affidavit, signed by the record
owner of the property, that includes a description of the primary dwelling unit; a statement

that the primary dwelling unit contains an internal accessory dwelling unit or that the
property contains a detached ADU, as applicable; and a statement that the ADU may only
be used in accordance with the city’s land use regulations. Change in ownership of the
primary dwelling shall not require any additional public hearing, but shall require an
updated ADU permit, site inspection (if applicable), and signed affidavit.
19.75.070 Inspection
A. Prior to approval of an ADU permit, all required building permits shall be completed
by the applicant and inspected by the city’s building inspector to verify compliance
with all applicable city standards.
B. If no additional work is proposed or required to ready an ADU for occupancy, the
applicant shall submit a minimum-fee building permit application, accompanied by
an inspection by the city’s building inspector, to ensure compliance with all
applicable standards.
19.75.080 Time Limits
Unless subsequent steps in the approval process of an ADU permit are undertaken within
six months after the most recent step If the ADU permit application remains idle for six
months, said permit shall expire.
19.75.090 Termination
If the primary dwelling’s record owner changes and is not accompanied by a new ADU
application, or if the primary dwelling’s record owner is no longer permanently residing in
the primary dwelling, then the ADU shall be immediately vacated and shall no longer be
used as an ADU. The city may revoke, or may choose to deny license renewal, to any
property with unresolved violations of this code arising from or related to operation of an
ADU. The city may also hold a lien against a property that contains an internal ADU that
violated this chapter pursuant to the procedures detailed in UTAH CODE ANN. 10-21303(4)10-9a-530(5), as amended, and may pursue any other remedies available at law for
violations involving a detached ADU.

Utah Code

Effective 11/6/2025
10-21-303 Internal accessory dwelling units.
(1) In any area zoned primarily for residential use:
(a) the use of an internal accessory dwelling unit is a permitted use;
(b) except as provided in Subsections (2) and (3), a municipality may not establish any
restrictions or requirements for the construction or use of one internal accessory dwelling unit
within a primary dwelling, including a restriction or requirement governing:
(i) the size of the internal accessory dwelling unit in relation to the primary dwelling;
(ii) total lot size;
(iii) street frontage; or
(iv) internal connectivity; and
(c) a municipality's regulation of architectural elements for internal accessory dwelling units shall
be consistent with the regulation of single-family units, including single-family units located in
historic districts.
(2) An internal accessory dwelling unit shall comply with all applicable building, health, and fire
codes.
(3) A municipality may:
(a) prohibit the installation of a separate utility meter for an internal accessory dwelling unit;
(b) require that an internal accessory dwelling unit be designed in a manner that does not change
the appearance of the primary dwelling as a single-family dwelling;
(c) require a primary dwelling:
(i) regardless of whether the primary dwelling is existing or new construction, to include one
additional on-site parking space for an internal accessory dwelling unit, in addition to the
parking spaces required under the municipality's land use regulation, except that if the
municipality's land use ordinance requires four off-street parking spaces, the municipality
may not require the additional space contemplated under this Subsection (3)(c)(i); and
(ii) to replace any parking spaces contained within a garage or carport if an internal accessory
dwelling unit is created within the garage or carport and is a habitable space;
(d) prohibit the creation of an internal accessory dwelling unit within a mobile home as defined in
Section 57-16-3;
(e) require the owner of a primary dwelling to obtain a permit or license for renting an internal
accessory dwelling unit;
(f) prohibit the creation of an internal accessory dwelling unit within a zoning district covering an
area that is equivalent to:
(i) 25% or less of the total area in the municipality that is zoned primarily for residential use,
except that the municipality may not prohibit newly constructed internal accessory dwelling
units that:
(A) have a final plat approval dated on or after October 1, 2021; and
(B) comply with applicable land use regulations; or
(ii) 67% or less of the total area in the municipality that is zoned primarily for residential use, if
the main campus of a state or private university with a student population of 10,000 or more
is located within the municipality;
(g) prohibit the creation of an internal accessory dwelling unit if the primary dwelling is served by
a failing septic tank;
(h) prohibit the creation of an internal accessory dwelling unit if the lot containing the primary
dwelling is 6,000 square feet or less in size;
(i) prohibit the rental or offering the rental of an internal accessory dwelling unit for a period of
less than 30 consecutive days;
Page 1

Utah Code

(j) prohibit the rental of an internal accessory dwelling unit if the internal accessory dwelling unit
is located in a dwelling that is not occupied as the owner's primary residence;
(k) hold a lien against a property that contains an internal accessory dwelling unit in accordance
with Subsection (4); and
(l) record a notice for an internal accessory dwelling unit in accordance with Subsection (5).
(4)
(a) In addition to any other legal or equitable remedies available to a municipality, a municipality
may hold a lien against a property that contains an internal accessory dwelling unit if:
(i) the owner of the property violates any of the provisions of this section or any ordinance
adopted under Subsection (3);
(ii) the municipality provides a written notice of violation in accordance with Subsection (4)(b);
(iii) the municipality holds a hearing and determines that the violation has occurred in
accordance with Subsection (4)(d), if the owner files a written objection in accordance with
Subsection (4)(b)(iv);
(iv) the owner fails to cure the violation within the time period prescribed in the written notice of
violation under Subsection (4)(b);
(v) the municipality provides a written notice of lien in accordance with Subsection (4)(c); and
(vi) the municipality records a copy of the written notice of lien described in Subsection (4)(a)(v)
with the county recorder of the county in which the property is located.
(b) The written notice of violation shall:
(i) describe the specific violation;
(ii) provide the owner of the internal accessory dwelling unit a reasonable opportunity to cure
the violation that is:
(A) no less than 14 days after the day on which the municipality sends the written notice
of violation, if the violation results from the owner renting or offering to rent the internal
accessory dwelling unit for a period of less than 30 consecutive days; or
(B) no less than 30 days after the day on which the municipality sends the written notice of
violation, for any other violation;
(iii) state that if the owner of the property fails to cure the violation within the time period
described in Subsection (4)(b)(ii), the municipality may hold a lien against the property in an
amount of up to $100 for each day of violation after the day on which the opportunity to cure
the violation expires;
(iv) notify the owner of the property:
(A) that the owner may file a written objection to the violation within 14 days after the day on
which the written notice of violation is post-marked or posted on the property; and
(B) of the name and address of the municipal office where the owner may file the written
objection;
(v) be mailed to:
(A) the property's owner of record; and
(B) any other individual designated to receive notice in the owner's license or permit records;
and
(vi) be posted on the property.
(c) The written notice of lien shall:
(i) comply with the requirements of Section 38-12-102;
(ii) state that the property is subject to a lien;
(iii) specify the lien amount, in an amount of up to $100 for each day of violation after the day
on which the opportunity to cure the violation expires;
(iv) be mailed to:
Page 2

Utah Code

(A) the property's owner of record; and
(B) any other individual designated to receive notice in the owner's license or permit records;
and
(v) be posted on the property.
(d)
(i) If an owner of property files a written objection in accordance with Subsection (4)(b)(iv), the
municipality shall:
(A) hold a hearing in accordance with Title 52, Chapter 4, Open and Public Meetings Act,
to conduct a review and determine whether the specific violation described in the written
notice of violation under Subsection (4)(b) has occurred; and
(B) notify the owner in writing of the date, time, and location of the hearing described in
Subsection (4)(d)(i)(A) no less than 14 days before the day on which the hearing is held.
(ii) If an owner of property files a written objection under Subsection (4)(b)(iv), a municipality
may not record a lien under this Subsection (4) until the municipality holds a hearing and
determines that the specific violation has occurred.
(iii) If the municipality determines at the hearing that the specific violation has occurred, the
municipality may impose a lien in an amount of up to $100 for each day of violation after the
day on which the opportunity to cure the violation expires, regardless of whether the hearing
is held after the day on which the opportunity to cure the violation has expired.
(e) If an owner cures a violation within the time period prescribed in the written notice of violation
under Subsection (4)(b), the municipality may not hold a lien against the property, or impose
any penalty or fee on the owner, in relation to the specific violation described in the written
notice of violation under Subsection (4)(b).
(5)
(a) A municipality that issues, on or after October 1, 2021, a permit or license to an owner of a
primary dwelling to rent an internal accessory dwelling unit, or a building permit to an owner
of a primary dwelling to create an internal accessory dwelling unit, may record a notice in the
office of the recorder of the county in which the primary dwelling is located.
(b) The notice described in Subsection (5)(a) shall include:
(i) a description of the primary dwelling;
(ii) a statement that the primary dwelling contains an internal accessory dwelling unit; and
(iii) a statement that the internal accessory dwelling unit may only be used in accordance with
the municipality's land use regulations.
(c) The municipality shall, upon recording the notice described in Subsection (5)(a), deliver a
copy of the notice to the owner of the internal accessory dwelling unit.

Effective 10/1/2026
10-21-304 Detached accessory dwelling units.
(1)
(a) A specified municipality shall adopt a land use regulation that permits a detached accessory
dwelling unit on any lot or parcel that is 11,000 square feet or larger and contains a singlefamily dwelling, if the single-family dwelling is a permitted use on the lot or parcel.
(b) This section does not prohibit a municipality from adopting a land use regulation that permits
a detached accessory dwelling unit on a lot or parcel that is smaller than 11,000 square feet.
(2) A land use regulation described in Subsection (1) shall:
(a) require that a detached accessory dwelling unit comply with all applicable building, health,
and fire codes; and
(b) include a process for the owner of a legally constructed accessory structure to convert the
accessory structure to a detached accessory dwelling unit subject to applicable:
(i) dwelling and accessory structure setback requirements; and
(ii) building, health, and fire codes.
(3) A land use regulation described in Subsection (1) may not:
(a) require a conditional use permit for a detached accessory dwelling unit if the proposed
detached accessory dwelling unit is located in a primarily residential zone;
(b) require more than two on-site parking spaces assigned to a detached accessory dwelling unit
that is 650 square feet or larger;
(c) require more than one on-site parking space assigned to a detached accessory dwelling unit
that is smaller than 650 square feet; or
(d) include design standards for a detached accessory dwelling unit that conflict with Section
10-20-618.
(4) A land use regulation described in Subsection (1) may:
(a) require a detached accessory dwelling unit to:
(i) conform to applicable land use regulations that regulate structure size, dimension, height,
and maximum lot coverage;
(ii) conform to setback requirements, that may take into account proximity to property lines and
other structures, easements, window orientation, massing, or other elements; and
(iii) be designed consistent with the design of the single-family dwelling;
(b) prohibit a detached accessory dwelling unit from being:
(i) larger in size than the single-family dwelling located on the same lot or parcel;
(ii) located within a public utility easement or other recorded easement;
(iii) located in a front-yard area of a lot or parcel; or
(iv) rented for less than 90 consecutive days;
(c) require that the owner of a lot or parcel where a detached accessory dwelling unit is located
reside in the detached single-family dwelling or detached accessory dwelling unit located on
the lot or parcel;
(d) require that when a detached garage is converted to a detached accessory dwelling unit, any
parking spaces required for the single-family dwelling that were located within the detached
garage are replaced on-site;
(e) prohibit more than one accessory dwelling unit on a lot or parcel; and
(f) prohibit a detached accessory dwelling unit if:
(i) the detached accessory dwelling unit will not have adequate access to a required utility
service that is a project improvement, including sanitary sewer, culinary water, electrical, or
storm water; or

Page 1

Utah Code

(ii) a utility service that is a system improvement, including sanitary sewer, culinary water,
electrical, or storm water, to which the detached accessory dwelling unit is required to
connect does not have sufficient capacity to support the addition of the detached accessory
dwelling unit to the utility service system improvements.
(5) This section does not supersede:
(a) a land use regulation that regulates a detached accessory building that is not a detached
accessory dwelling unit;
(b) prohibitions or restrictions on detached accessory dwelling units in a development agreement
signed by a municipality on or before May 6, 2026; or
(c) a land use regulation or administrative action that:
(i) is not prohibited by law; and
(ii) relates to a detached accessory dwelling unit.

WORK SESSION
Chair Sean Steinman called the Planning Commission Work Session to order at 5:00 p.m.
Community and Economic Development Director, Jim Spung introduced new Planning
Technician, Landon Kraczek, who recently graduated from the University of Utah, where he
obtained a master’s degree in planning with an emphasis on urban design.
Mr. Kraczek stated that he was excited to be part of Cottonwood Heights. He is a member of the
Salt Lake City Planning Commission and was previously its chair. He enjoys creating spaces for
people to join together in community. The world had become stratified, with pockets of people
isolated in their home, and planning was a way to redirect energy toward community and
connection. He helped build the underpass park in Salt Lake City and was leading a project to
activate its Main Street with seven bee statues. In response to a question from Chair Steinman,
Mr. Kraczek stated that he received a grant from the Downtown Alliance for the bee statues.

Review Business Session Agenda.

The Business Session Agenda was reviewed.
Planner III, Maverick Yeh reported that Item 3.2 was Project CUP-26-016, an application for a
Conditional Use Permit (“CUP”) for the Lovein Nest Childcare Home Occupation at 7164 South
Ponderosa Drive. The childcare would have up to 12 children under the age of five, and the hours
of operation were Monday through Friday from 7:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m.
The subject property was zoned R-1-8 Residential Single-Family. Properties to the west were
zoned Regional Commercial (“CR”), and properties to the south were zoned R-2-8 Residential
Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 10/07/26

1

Multi-Family. The Applicant proposed to use the home’s living room and master bedroom as
designated childcare areas, with the backyard designated as an outdoor play area. A compliant
fence and gate would be installed prior to use.
Staff reviewed applicable home daycare or preschool standards and determined the following:

Up to 12 children are allowed, including qualifying caregiver children.
No more than one nonresident employee was allowed at any one time, and only one

traffic and parking impacts. Client parking would be accommodated in the existing driveway.

review and approval.

•

•

The property is in the R-1-8 Single-Family Residential zoning district.
A Home Occupation with clients may be approved as a Conditional Use in the R-1-8 Zone
pursuant to CHMC §§ 19.26.030(E) and 19.76.040(F)(7).
RESYNC LC would provide massage therapy within the existing residence and be owneroperated with no additional employees.
The business anticipates approximately two to three clients per day, with no more than one
client on the premises at a time. Appointments would be staggered to minimize traffic and
overlapping arrivals.
Client parking would be accommodated in the existing circular driveway. The Community
and Economic Development Director determines whether parking beyond the spaces
required for the dwelling is need.
The proposed business would operate indoors, with no exterior signage or outdoor business
activity. The use must remain incidental and secondary to the residential use.
Staff found that, subject to the Conditions of Approval, the limited scale and indoor nature
of the use were expected to minimize offsite impacts and preserve the residential character
of the neighborhood consistent with the Conditional Use Standards in CHMC § 19.84.080.
One public comment was received asking that all parking be on the property.

2.0

CUP-25-005 – Old Mill Demolition.

Mr. Spung reported that the owner of the Old Mill applied for a CUP to demolish the structure in
summer 2025. As it was a designated Historic Structure, additional review was required. As part
of the review, a public hearing was held on January 21, 2026, and the Planning Commission was
prohibited from making a decision on the application until one year from that date. During that
time, Staff had collected data on the application and history of the structure. The property owner
had also recently submitted a business review including the history of the structure and different
business ventures at the location.
In spring 2026, the City hired a third-party consultant to perform a structural analysis of the Old
Mill to determine its current state and potential paths forward. Dunn Associates, Inc., would
present their findings and recommendations during the Business Session.
The next public hearing on the item would occur in January or February 2027. In the interim, Staff
would consolidate all information received over the last year for Planning Commission discussion
and review prior to a formal motion to approve, deny, or approve the request with conditions.
A new Chair and Vice-Chair would also be elected during the Business Session. Mr. Spung asked
that each Commissioner write down their choices. City Recorder, Sydney Pierce would then count
the votes and report on the results. Each position serves a one-year term, and a Commissioner may
serve in the position for two consecutive terms.

Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 10/07/26

6

2.0

General Public Comment

Chair Steinman opened the public comment period.
Evan Chan stated that she had been working with neighbors on ways to preserve the Old Mill. She
thanked the property owner and Walker Development for working closely with the grassroots
organization. They were clearly interested in preserving the Old Mill. She had asked ChatGPT
for a list of the 40 most significant pre-1900 buildings in Utah. Out of 40, only three had been
restored by private interests. The rest were either owned by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latterday Saints, nonprofit organizations, or the government, which showed how challenging it would
be for Cottonwood Heights or Walker Development to find the money to restore the Old Mill. She
urged the State government, a religious organization, or a large foundation to step in and preserve
the building, which was made of the same material as the Salt Lake Temple and is the fourth-oldest
industrial building in Utah. It is a very significant part of Utah history, and she hoped to work
with the Planning Commission and City Council to broaden the reach and try to save the building.
A petition to save the Old Mill was available on Change.org and had garnered 300 signatures over
the past month. She had posters available and encouraged those present to take one to share with
their neighbors and organizations that are interested in saving historic buildings.
Kevin Witzenman stated that the application to demolish the Old Mill rested on two central claims:
that the building had no real foundation and could not be salvaged, and that the City condemned it
in 2005. A review of the underlying records showed that neither claim was adequately supported.
The claim that there was no foundation had not been verified. The owner’s engineer asserted that
the granite walls rest on the ground without footings, rendering the structure unsalvageable, but no
subsurface investigation had been conducted. There had been no test pits at the base of the walls,
geotechnical borings, or soil testing. The most recent engineering evaluation was a limited visual
screening based on the observation and drawings only and stated that foundation elements were
not believed to be present, an assumption rather than a verified finding. An earlier engineering
report concluded that the building could be salvaged with structural upgrades, and a masonry
restoration contractor who inspected it stated he was confident that it sat on a stone foundation.
He personally offered to fund an independent engineering assessment of the building. Casey
Sullivan, a masonry restoration contractor, offered to survey the structure and check the foundation
at his own expense. Neither offer was taken up. As a result, the central factual question of what
was beneath the walls remained unanswered, even though the means to answer was available at no
cost to the City or owner.
The building was never formally condemned. It was widely repeated in news coverage,
preservation materials, and reference resources that the City condemned the Old Mill in 2005, but
that claim traced to a single uncited statement with no supporting documentation. At the January
21st, 2026, public hearing, both the City Attorney and the Applicant’s attorney stated on record
that the building had never been formally condemned. The City Attorney further stated that the
City had never condemned any property, and no condemnation order or unsafe building notice had
been produced. The record, including the current engineering report, should be corrected or the
condemnation documented.

Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 10/07/26

7

The cost figures were not repair estimates. The commonly cited figures of $45 million to over
$100 million were not estimates to repair the building. The $45 million figure reflected the cost
of constructing an entirely new building.
Jesse Allen stated that he is an architect and landscape architect who lives in District 4. He
currently served on the Architectural Review Commission and was previously a member of the
Planning Commission. He was excited to hear the results of the structural analysis. The Old Mill
is a historic landmark in the community, and he hoped that the landowners would reconsider the
demolition permit, and the City Council and Planning Commission found its historic significance
as reason to preserve the structure to some degree. He believed there was a range of options, from
a full structural rebuild to salvaging the historic ruins by removing modern additions and
stabilizing what remains. The Old Mill Art Museum in Minneapolis, Minnesota was a great
example of stabilizing the ruins of an old mill and building a multi-story art museum next to it.
His hope was the landowner, philanthropic organizations, government, and everyone involved
review the full range of possibilities for the amazing historical landmark structure.
Shawna Bland stated that she and her husband had lived in Old Mill Estates for many years. They
love it there and do not want to see it become crowded with townhomes and condominiums.
Everyone in the City loves the Old Mill, and for decades they have watched it become more and
more dilapidated. The owners never spent money to repair it, and she was sure they would love
nothing more than to tear it down and put in condominiums and townhomes, but there was a need
for single-family homes. There were townhomes and apartment buildings everywhere, so there
was plenty of that type of housing. She did not want to see Cottonwood Heights become
overdeveloped like so many cities in Utah.
Jackie Hibbard reported that she resides in Old Mill Estates and loves it there. She thanked Doug
Shelby for donating the land and the City for the trails. She implored the City to think about what
would be built in place of the Old Mill. The trails were priceless, and there was not much open
space left. Single-family homes would be best. American Fork was just townhomes and apartment
buildings, and she was worried about people raising their children in townhomes. The Old Mill
property was one of the last pristine areas left, and she hoped the City and Mr. Shelby would be
mindful about what goes there.
Allen Fletcher stated that he had lived in Old Mill Estates and driven past the Old Mill for over 30
years. He felt sympathy for Mr. Shelby, who he considered a friend. Everyone wanted to save the
Old Mill, but what would they do with it? For 15 years, people had tried to figure out what to do
with it, but it must serve some purpose. He believed there was a middle ground where the Old
Mill could be developed or turned into a structurally safe memorial. He did not believe that
building it out with townhomes and condominiums would be a good use of the land. There is one
road in and out, and people could be stuck there in an emergency. There are already single-family
homes in the area, and he believed they should build more with perhaps smaller lots, so the
neighborhood is contiguous. That would make things easier in an emergency as well as for school
bus traffic. He believed there was a middle ground where portions could be preserved as a
memorial and Mr. Shelby could take the Old Mill apart and do something safe with it.

Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 10/07/26

8

Dan Hammer of Walker Development stated that the family would love to preserve the Old Mill
but did not have the financial wherewithal to do so. They also viewed it as a hazard and a danger.
If there was another solution, they would be happy to consider it. They had offered the Old Mill
to the City, but they did not want the liability because they considered it a dangerous nuisance and
were worried that someone would get hurt there. They had offered a middle ground where the
City would identify elements of the Old Mill to preserve and keep, and those elements would be
preserved in the new city center. Regarding future development, conversations about density
would occur later, and the City could decide what was appropriate for the area at that time. The
application was about demolition of the Old Mill, not future development.
There were no further comments. The public comment period was closed.

The Applicant, Bayan Arian, reported that Lovein Nest would be a small, licensed home daycare
and preschool serving children under the age of five, with no more than 12 children and no nonresident employee. Her goal was to provide a safe, organized, and nurturing environment for
young children while maintaining the residential character of the neighborhood.
She had worked carefully to address the City’s concerns regarding parking, traffic, outdoor
activity, and noise. The Parking and Circulation Plan was revised and approved by the Community
and Economic Development Director. Drop-off and pick-up times would be scheduled based on
family schedules and needs so arrivals and departures remained organized and did not create
congestion or queueing on Ponderosa Drive. Because the children are young, outdoor play would
be structured, supervised, and limited. She anticipated a short outdoor play period in late morning
and another later in the afternoon. The backyard would be fully fenced and gated prior to use for
childcare in compliance with applicable City and Utah childcare licensing requirements.
Ms. Arian understood that it was a residential neighborhood and was committed to operating
Lovein Nest respectfully, following all applicable City regulations, childcare licensing
requirements, noise regulations, and the conditions of the CUP.
In response to a question from Chair Steinman, Ms. Arian reported that drop-off and pick-up times
would be scheduled based on the parents’ schedule, and those activities would take between five
and ten minutes to complete. The driveway is large and can accommodate three vehicles at a time.
If a fourth parent arrived outside of their scheduled time, there was space for them to wait on the
property. Space is also available in the garage during the day. Chair Steinman asked how she
would accommodate the request if all 12 parents chose 7:45 a.m. as their drop-off time. Ms. Arian
stated that she did not anticipate that issue as she would speak with the parents to create a schedule.
She was comfortable with any additional conditions set by the Planning Commission.
In response to a question raised by Commissioner Smith, Ms. Arian reported that the youngest
child in her care would be eight weeks old.

Condition 5 is modified to allow no more than two client vehicles on premises at
any one time unless the curb cut is extended to allow for a third vehicle.

Commissioner Shelton seconded the motion. Vote on Motion: Commissioner Smith-Yes;
Commissioner Shelton-Yes; Commissioner Barnes-Yes; Commissioner Kovac-Yes;
Commissioner Crowder-Yes; Commissioner Petersen-Yes; Commissioner Smith-Yes;
Commissioner Shelton-Yes; Chair Steinman-Yes. The motion passed with the unanimous
consent of the Commission.

3.3

Project CUP-26-015 - The Planning Commission will hold a public hearing to
consider a request for a Conditional Use Permit submitted by ReAnne Cram
& Brett Clark to operate a home occupation with client visits, providing a
home massage business, at 7640 South 2325 East.

Ms. Glende presented the Staff Report and stated that the request is for a CUP to operate RESYNC
LC, a Home Occupation with clients at 7640 South 2325 East. The business would provide private
massage therapy sessions within an existing room of the residence. There would be no additional
employees. The business would serve two to three clients per day, with no more than one client
on premises at any one time and staggered appointments to minimize traffic and parking impacts.
Client parking would be accommodated in the existing driveway. Proposed hours were Monday
through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. No exterior modifications, signage, outdoor business
activities, or structural improvement were proposed. The Applicant has expressed interest in a
future office addition, which would require separate City approval.
A zoning and Impact analysis determined the following:
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

The property is in the R-1-8 Single-Family Residential zoning district.
A Home Occupation with clients may be approved as a Conditional Use in the R-1-8 Zone.
RESYNC LC would provide massage therapy within the existing residence and be owneroperated with no additional employees.
The business anticipates approximately two to three clients per day, with no more than one
client on the premises at a time. Appointments would be staggered to minimize traffic and
overlapping arrivals.
Client parking would be accommodated in the existing circular driveway.
The proposed business would operate indoors, with no exterior signage or outdoor business
activity. The use must remain incidental and secondary to the residential use.
Staff found that, subject to the Conditions of Approval, the limited scale and indoor nature
of the use were expected to minimize offsite impacts and preserve the residential character
of the neighborhood.
One public comment was received asking that all client parking be accommodated within
the driveway.

Staff recommended approval with the following conditions:
1.
2.
3.
4.

The Applicant shall obtain and maintain a valid Cottonwood Heights Business
License for the duration of the Home Occupation.
The Home Occupation shall operate only within the existing residence and shall
remain clearly incidental and secondary to the primary residential use of the
property.
The business shall be owner-operated with no additional employees or independent
contractors conducting business on the premises.
The Home Occupation shall operate by appointment only and shall be limited to
the following hours as described in the approved application: Monday through
Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

The Home Occupation shall be limited to providing massage therapy services as

The business shall serve no more than one client at a time on the premises.
Appointments shall be scheduled and staggered to minimize traffic, parking, and

Approval of this Conditional use Permit is subject to review or revocation upon
evidence of noncompliance with these conditions or applicable provisions of the
Cottonwood Heights Municipal Code.
Any expansion or modification of the Home Occupation, including but not limited
to hours of operation, number of clients served, services provided, parking
arrangements, or employment of additional personnel shall require additional City
review and approval prior to implementation.

The Applicant, ReAnne Cram stated that she and her husband own the property. She appreciated

stay in compliance. In response to his question, Ms. Cram clarified that she would avoid

10:00 p.m. would be more than sufficient as she preferred not to work past 6:00 p.m. In response
to a follow-up question from Commissioner Smith, she confirmed that she would be pleased to
extend the hours from 7:30 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.

3.4

Project CUP-25-005.
The third-party study team will present the Old Mill Structural Analysis
Report and its findings.

Mr. Spung introduced Tyler Wright of Dunn Associates, Inc. and indicated that Sean Flynn of
Aegis Consulting was present online.
Mr. Wright presented the Old Mill Structural Analysis. Dunn Associates, Inc. was hired by the
City to provide a structural analysis of the Cottonwood Heights Paper Mill, as well as cost
estimates to bring the historic structure back into operation.
A photograph of the original mill was displayed, and Mr. Wright remarked that the existing
building had never operated as a mill as it was reconstructed after a fire. Photographs of the
structure’s existing condition were reviewed next. A drone was used to analyze the interior as the
roof had collapsed and the building’s current condition was not safe for entry.
The following key structural deficiencies and recommendations were discussed:
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

While some original granite remained, anything rebuilt after the fire was presumed to be
brick.
The walls were too tall and slender, which created a tendency to bow during large seismic
events.
Anchorage between the walls and floor was inadequate as the load could not transfer from
the floor to the walls and there was nothing to hold the walls onto the rest of the building.
There were no secondary columns to support vertical loads.
Due to the amount of weathering, the structure lacked structural integrity.
Much of the roof was collapsed and in need of extensive repairs.
The masonry towers required rebuilding or bracing.
It was unlikely that foundation footings had been restrained by concrete beams.
The site had slope constraints and was very close to a known fault.

Preservation options were reviewed next.
Option 1: Stabilize in Place
•
•

New steel bracing structure
Local footings to support bracing

Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 10/07/26

16

•
•

No public access
Further weathering would occur with this option.

Option 2: Repair and Restore
•
•
•
•

Temporarily stabilize granite masonry
Reframe floors and roof with adequate anchorage to walls
Provide new concrete shear walls on inside of masonry with new footings
South courtyard walls must be either stabilized or removed.

Option 3: Rebuild in Historic Form
•
•
•
•
•

Strategically demolish the existing building
Catalog and store granite
Rebuild in the footprint of the original building
New layout to meet building codes and new use
Utility the granite as veneer to recreate the exterior.

Mr. Flynn discussed the average estimated cost and potential return on investment for each option.
•
•
•

Option 1: $7.5 to $8.3 million
o There would be no public use or rental income from this option.
Option 2: $42.8 million
Option 3: $46.3 million
o These costs were broken down in detail in the full report, including yearly
escalation and tenant-improvement costs of approximately $6 million.

If only the structure were restored to its historic form, the property owner should expect an
approximately $11 million loss. If restored within a master development, approximately $5
million in income could be expected, which would bring the total loss to $6 million. To break
even, they would need to decrease the rebuild costs to approximately $42 million, increase lease
rates to $38 per square foot per year, and potentially capture shared costs in one master budget.
In response to a question raised by Commissioner Shelton, Mr. Wright reported that they had the
previous structural analyses but did not pull from them. However, based on buildings from the
era, the structure was unlikely to have a concrete foundation. It was more likely to have a stone
foundation. It was also possible that the walls just stopped at the ground. There are ways to
strengthen and repair foundations on historic buildings.
Commissioner Shelton asked about the load path references in the report. Mr. Wright reported
that from a load path standpoint, they look at whether the floor makes it to the ground. There is
sometimes a bearing wall with nothing below it. In this case, the floor and roof framing spread to
the walls, which went directly down to the ground. The type of foundation was in question, but
whether it could hold current loads was not in question because visual observation identified no
large areas of settlement.

Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 10/07/26

17

Commissioner Shelton asked if the building in its current state represented a risk to health, safety,
and welfare. Mr. Wright stated that his firm was not prepared to answer the question at the time
as it would require additional onsite investigation. It was obvious that some elements were in need
of repair, but they were not tasked with answering that question.
Chair Steinman asked about next steps. Mr. Wright reported that the City, property owner, and
any potential development partners needed to work together to determine them. Step 1 was to
consider whether the structure was economically viable, which was answered in the report.
Whether it could be developed was a much larger discussion.
Commissioner Shelton asked if the proximity to known mapped faults would prohibit
development. Mr. Wright reported that development would be permitted. Seismic hazard
increases with proximity to a fault, and half of the structure was in a special study zone. If it was
moved 200 feet to the west, it would be outside of that zone. However, it was not directly on top
of a fault. In response to Commissioner Shelton’s follow-up question, he stated that he was not
aware of the City’s fault setback standards, but he believed the location may be beyond any setback
requirements from mapped faults.
Mr. Spung explained that the property was within the Sensitive Lands Overlay District. Before
development could occur, the property owner would be required to perform a geotechnical hazards
study to verify fault line locations and whether any hazards were present. The report would
delineate what type of setback would be required based on the type of structure, occupancy, etc.
There would likely be some impact, but their extent was unknown until a study was completed.
Commissioner Shelton asked if it was possible to permit new construction on the site. Mr. Spung
confirmed that it was possible. Buildings were allowed in the Gravel Pit and Canyon Centre, and
both properties had fault lines running through them. He believed the setback requirement was
between 20 to 50 feet, and there was not a fault line in that proximity to the Old Mill. Mr. Wright
stated that the study zone pertained to the Gravel Pit fault, which was on the east side of Wasatch
Boulevard. Mr. Spung added that the geotechnical engineer would perform trenching to confirm
that there were no unmapped faults present on the property.
Commissioner Kovac asked if a geotechnical survey was considered in the cost estimates outlined
in the report. Mr. Wright stated that it would be an additional cost but was a smaller, softer cost
relative to the hard cost of construction. The estimates also assumed that the current property
owner would develop the property. No transactional costs were included.
Chair Steinman asked about the anticipated land basis. Mr. Flynn reported that the development
proforma was based on a lease, so land value was not applicable to the analysis. They considered
a dining, event, or restaurant space based on anticipated market conditions. Other development
opportunities could be considered but were not part of the analysis. They believed it was a master
development opportunity, which would not recognize its full value until approximately year 10.
Chair Steinman asked what studies were conducted to determine that a dining or event space was
the highest and best use for the structure. Mr. Flynn stated that it was based on regional market
condition reports, as well as discussions with tenants who would be interested in that type of

Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 10/07/26

18

project. High-end restaurants had looked at the property and would love the opportunity. Chair
Steinman asked if a residential study was conducted. Mr. Wright reported that condominiums,
hotels, etc. would be part of a master development. This step looked solely at the building, but
many development scenarios could be considered for the property. They picked the most obvious
opportunity for the assignment.
Commissioner Crowder asked if restoring the property would make it less usable than rebuilding.
Mr. Wright reported that restoration was less advantageous from square footage and optimization
standpoints. There were multiple variables and scenarios. Mr. Flynn reported that there was an
approximately 20% inefficiency, as there would be dead space from bracing, etc. that would not
be present if the structure was rebuilt to current code. A new building could also be designed for
the end user and would not have the same constraints as the current structure. Commissioner
Crowder agreed but stated that it would still be a historic structure. Otherwise, they would be
investing in a new building at a loss.
Chair Steinman asked if there was a way to close the $6 million gap with a master development
with additional density. Mr. Flynn confirmed that it was possible as higher density means higher
valuation. Chair Steinman asked if changing the use from dining and events to residential would
close the gap without an additional master development. Mr. Flynn stated that it would need to be
analyzed with the development team as the study did not consider a residential component.
Mr. Spung pointed out that the cost estimates did not include any offsite utility or other costs that
would be required for the development. For example, the property was not in a steady pressure
zone for culinary water. Mr. Flynn confirmed that only the building was considered as aspects
like required water line size would vary based on the demands of the specific development.
Mr. Spung reported that the Planning Commission could not make a decision on the item until
January 2027. The City was still in a data-gathering phase so an informed decision could be made,
and the study was important to understand existing conditions. Over the next few months, Staff
would compile all information into a cohesive report for presentation at a 2027 public hearing.
Chair Steinman stated that many citizens and multiple news stations attended the initial public
hearing, and several people spoke in support of preservation and restoration of the Old Mill. He
asked if anyone had volunteered to fund the project. Mr. Spung indicated that no offers had been
made. The City was currently reviewing the application to demolish the historic structure, and any
third-party efforts were outside of the current task. The property was privately owned, and the
City was limited in what it could require the property owner to do.
After the Planning Commission made a determination on the Conditional Use, the Applicant would
apply for a Certificate of Appropriateness from the City Council. The Council would review and
vote on the request before a final demolition order could be granted. The Council has a different
set of review criteria than the Planning Commission and can consider issues like economic value.
Chair Steinman asked if the City had explored State funding opportunities for preservation of the
structure. Mr. Spung stated that there were likely grants available, but that was not the City’s role.

Cottonwood Heights Planning Commission Meeting – 10/07/26

19

The Old Mill was a community asset, but it was not community owned. Other groups had been
working with the property owner.
Chair Steinman thanked the Walker Family Trust and Mr. Shelby for continuing to provide
information to the City. It was not being taken lightly, and everyone wanted to ensure that the
appropriate next steps were taken.
